title: Go-to Guides
author: Latimir, Craig
summary: Craig Latimir describes developing "Go-to Guides," department-level planning documents that sit in the gap between a bare curriculum objective and an actual lesson, inspired by science-department booklets built by Pav Aujla. Walking through the circle-theorems guide as a worked example, he details each of its seven sections: an Overview translating curriculum objectives into plain English with cross-topic links; a "Topic Familiarisation" section of real exam questions, mark schemes, and examiner notes designed to reveal how a topic is actually assessed rather than just what it covers; a "Possible Models and Tips" section for pedagogical subject knowledge, common misconceptions, and teaching approaches; a Key Words section that explicitly distinguishes tier-2 vocabulary in common use from tier-3 maths-specific vocabulary; a Topic History and Hinterland section for the "rich stories" embedded in mathematics; a suggested Possible Learning Sequence; and a Resources section. He argues these guides fill a genuine void that gets less attention than either curriculum documents or individual lesson plans, and closes by sharing a blank template and worked examples for other departments to adapt.
points: Latimir's "Topic Familiarisation" section deliberately front-loads teachers with real past-paper questions before they plan, explicitly warning against teaching only to those specific questions rather than to the underlying skill they represent.

His tier-2/tier-3 vocabulary distinction addresses a specific misconception he names directly: teachers routinely misclassify common-usage words as maths-specific, missing opportunities to link vocabulary to students' existing knowledge from other contexts.

The Topic History and Hinterland section is framed as filling a specific gap, exposing the "diverse and global endeavour" behind mathematical ideas that gets lost when a topic is taught as a bare procedure.
Latimir positions the guides as occupying an underserved space between curriculum-level documents and lesson-level planning, rather than duplicating either.
quotes: There are so many more things beyond just a list of objectives taken directly from the National Curriculum that are needed to prepare someone to teach content well to a group of students.

This is designed to showcase some of the weird and wonderful ways that this content is assessed. It contains questions, mark scheme and any examiners notes. It should help direct the teaching to cover more than just a surface level understanding the topic.
One of the biggest misconceptions I think teachers have here is the sheer quantity of words that people think are tier 3 (maths specific) but are actually tier 2 (in common usage in other domains).
This is a chance for all those rich stories that are sometimes hidden in mathematics to come to life. This section contains relevant stories that have contributed to this part of the curriculum.
These guides are not lessons but sit in the void between the curriculum and lesson delivery that sometimes does not get nearly as much attention as it deserves.
